acceptedAnswer.text: Pregnancy itself does not directly cause tooth decay, but several factors associated with pregnancy can increase the risk. Morning sickness exposes teeth to stomach acid, which can erode enamel over time. Changes in dietary habits, including increased snacking and sugar cravings, can also contribute. Additionally, some women experience a reduction in saliva flow, which normally helps protect teeth by neutralising acids and washing away food particles. Maintaining a thorough oral hygiene routine, using fluoride toothpaste, and attending regular dental check-ups can help reduce the risk of decay during pregnancy.

mainEntity.name: Is it safe to have dental X-rays while pregnant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental X-rays are generally avoided during pregnancy as a precautionary measure, particularly during the first trimester. However, if there is an urgent clinical need — such as diagnosing an infection or a dental emergency — X-rays can be taken safely with appropriate protective shielding, including a lead apron. The radiation exposure from modern dental X-rays is very low. Your dentist will always weigh the potential benefits against any risks and will discuss the decision with you before proceeding. Non-urgent X-rays are typically postponed until after delivery.

mainEntity.name: Why do my gums bleed more during pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Increased gum bleeding during pregnancy is primarily caused by elevated hormone levels, particularly progesterone. These hormonal changes increase blood flow to the gum tissue and make it more reactive to plaque bacteria, leading to inflammation and a greater tendency to bleed during brushing or flossing. This condition, known as pregnancy gingivitis, affects many expectant mothers and is usually most noticeable during the second and third trimesters. Maintaining consistent brushing, flossing, and professional dental cleanings can help manage and reduce bleeding.

mainEntity.name: Should I visit the dentist during pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, visiting the dentist during pregnancy is recommended and considered safe. Routine check-ups and cleanings help maintain your oral health and allow your dentist to identify any developing concerns early. The second trimester is often the most comfortable time for dental appointments, but care can be provided throughout pregnancy. Be sure to inform your dental team about your pregnancy and any relevant medical information. In the UK, pregnant women are entitled to free NHS dental treatment, making it an ideal time to prioritise your dental health.

mainEntity.name: Can gum disease affect my baby?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some research has suggested a possible association between severe gum disease, known as periodontitis, and certain adverse pregnancy outcomes, including premature birth and low birth weight. The theory is that bacteria and inflammatory substances from infected gums may enter the bloodstream and potentially affect the pregnancy. However, this research is still developing, and many other factors influence pregnancy outcomes. While there is no need for alarm, maintaining good oral health during pregnancy is a sensible part of overall prenatal care and may offer protective benefits.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if I develop a lump on my gums during pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some pregnant women develop a localised swelling on the gums known as a pregnancy granuloma or pyogenic granuloma. This is a benign, non-cancerous growth that typically appears during the second trimester and is thought to be related to hormonal changes and the presence of plaque or tartar. These growths can bleed easily and may cause discomfort. In many cases, they resolve on their own after delivery. However, if the lump is causing significant discomfort or bleeding, your dentist can assess it and discuss management options, which may include professional cleaning or, in some cases, removal.
